text: You already know that in SQL Server, inserting a string too long for its column, or a NULL into a NOT NULL column, is always an error. There's no setting that changes that. MySQL is different. A system variable called sql_mode controls how strictly the server enforces rules like this, and it genuinely changes real server behavior, not just a warning level.

The first thing to do on any unfamiliar MySQL server: check its sql_mode. Select at-at sql_mode for the current session, or at-at GLOBAL dot sql_mode for the server-wide default. There's no single universal MySQL behavior — only MySQL behavior under whatever this particular server's sql_mode happens to be set to right now.

Here's the difference that bites hardest. Create a table with a five-character VARCHAR column. Without strict mode, inserting a ten-character string succeeds anyway, silently truncated down to five characters, with just a warning. Turn on STRICT_TRANS_TABLES, or STRICT_ALL_TABLES for non-transactional engines too, and that same insert becomes a hard error — the behavior you've always had in SQL Server, Oracle, and PostgreSQL.

Now here's one you'll recognize directly from your T-SQL background. Selecting CustomerId, CustomerName, count star, grouped only by CustomerId, is a hard error in T-SQL, because CustomerName isn't aggregated and isn't in the GROUP BY. Older MySQL, by default, let this run anyway, silently picking an arbitrary CustomerName per group — a real, silent data bug. Since MySQL five point seven, ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY ships on by default, finally enforcing the same rule T-SQL always has.

You can set sql_mode yourself. SET SESSION sql_mode, with a comma-separated list of modes, changes it just for your current connection. A permanent change means editing the server's configuration file, my dot cnf or my dot ini, under the mysqld section — not something you do with a SQL statement alone. Because this is configurable per server, the exact same query text can be perfectly fine on one MySQL install and throw a hard error on another.

Keep this in mind every time you move between MySQL environments: always check sql_mode before you trust that a query will behave the way it did somewhere else. Next lesson: MySQL stored procedures, and the DELIMITER trick you need to write one from the command-line client. See you there.
